content: The technician must be well-trained in relevant areas and should recognize when to consult the supervising clinician for review. Expanding the role of technicians to handle manufacturing tasks can help reduce service bottlenecks caused by the limited availability of qualified professionals. Support personnel, who may not have formal training in prosthetics or orthotics, play essential roles in non-clinical tasks such as plastic-forming or plaster work. Other support staff, such as storekeepers, cleaners, and maintenance workers, also contribute to the overall service delivery. Administrative personnel are often the first point of contact for users during appointments and follow-ups. Positive interactions with reception staff can significantly influence a user’s rehabilitation experience. Long-term users often develop friendly relationships with administrative personnel, which fosters a supportive environment. Targeted training for administrative staff may be necessary to maintain high service quality. Employing users in administrative roles can also provide opportunities for peer support, particularly for first-time users. Medical specialists are integral to prosthetics and orthotics services, often serving as part of a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team and referring users to appropriate services. Key specialists include physicians in physical and rehabilitation medicine, amputation surgery, orthopedics, vascular surgery, neurology, rheumatology, pediatrics, geriatrics, and other related fields. Physiotherapists and occupational therapists are critical to the success of prosthetics and orthotics services and should be permanent members of the multidisciplinary team, especially those specializing in areas such as amputation rehabilitation, stroke, cerebral palsy, clubfoot treatment, and spinal conditions. Other allied health professionals, such as podiatrists, psychologists, biomedical engineers, and pharmacists, also play important roles. In complex cases, prosthetics and orthotics services should be delivered by a multidisciplinary team with shared goals and a unified identity. These teams assess users’ needs, develop holistic treatment plans, and evaluate outcomes. Ideally, the team includes a prosthetist or orthotist, physician, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, nurse, psychologist, and social worker. Users and their families should also be considered part of the team, with the ability to influence decisions. In resource-limited settings, the team may be smaller, consisting of just the user and one rehabilitation professional. Training programs should be integrated into national health education systems and offered alongside courses for other rehabilitation professionals. Education combines theoretical and practical training, with students introduced to clinical practice in controlled environments before supervised placements. Training for technicians focuses on product preparation and the use of materials, tools, and machines. Various levels of training should be available to meet national demands, and pathways should allow for progression to higher levels of responsibility. Prosthetics and orthotics training programs should adhere to international and national educational standards, including those set by the International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics (ISPO). Theoretical training covers clinical subjects like anatomy, physiology, and biomechanics, while practical training emphasizes skills in design, production, and alignment. Students should develop problem-solving abilities, professional communication skills, and a commitment to continuous learning. Courses should also address user-centered care, disability issues, teamwork, professional ethics, and management tools. Selection of students for training should be transparent and based on academic criteria, ensuring they have the aptitude for clinical and technical work. Efforts should be made to balance gender representation and include individuals from diverse cultural and demographic backgrounds. Special initiatives may be needed to encourage women and people with disabilities to pursue training, as their inclusion can improve service accessibility and challenge negative attitudes. New graduates, after completing their training and internships, should receive support from senior professionals to gain experience and transition into independent practice. International training exposes students to diverse methods and contexts but may limit clinical practice in their home settings. Graduates returning from international programs may need additional support to integrate into their local professional environment. Continuing professional development (CPD) is essential for maintaining and enhancing competence. CPD can include formal courses, informal learning, and participation in seminars and workshops. It helps professionals stay updated on new technologies and practices, extend their knowledge, and specialize in specific areas. Access to scientific literature and training in research appraisal are crucial for fostering evidence-based practice. This collaboration can include preparing training modules and participating as lecturers.
